newsitem.title: USA: U.S. hog producers set plan to control farm odors.
newsitem.headline: U.S. hog producers set plan to control farm odors.

text.p: U.S. pork producer groups will fund two programs costing $5 million over the next 18 months to help hog farmers manage odor problems at their operations, pork industry officials said.
"Clearly, odor is one of the most pressing issues facing the modern pork industry," Jerry King, president of the National Pork Producers Council (NPPC), said at the industry's annual Pork Forum here.
King said the NPPC, in cooperation with the National Pork Board, has approved two programs to help producers manage the problem and provide rewards for putting solutions in place.
"We believe the technology exists today to minimize pork production odor at existing facilities but for a number of reasons it has not been widely employed," King said.

The first, an Odor Solutions Initiative, will be funded at $3.5 million. The goal is to solicit plans from producers for "practical, economical and sustainable technology" that the pork industry can use in manure and lagoon management.
Entries for the program will be due February 1, 1998.

A second program, funded at $1.5 million, will provide on-farm odor management assistance to pork producers. This program will employ environmental experts to visit hog farms and identify and implement odor control practices.
"We are convinced that small and medium-sized pork producers will be the major beneficiaries of these two unique program efforts," King said.

The moves come at a time when pork producers from Iowa to North Carolina are under increasing attack from environmental, consumer and civic groups seeking new regulations for odor control, waste management and soil management at big hog farms.
